# The model

`lpplsF` calibrates the log-periodic power law singularity (LPPLS) model, which
describes the faster-than-exponential growth of a speculative bubble, decorated
by oscillations that accelerate towards its end. In the parameterisation of
Filimonov and Sornette (2013), the log-price before a critical time $t_c$ is

$$
\ln p(t) = A + (t_c - t)^m \bigl[ B + C_1 \cos(\omega \ln(t_c - t))
  + C_2 \sin(\omega \ln(t_c - t)) \bigr], \qquad t < t_c .
$$

The critical time $t_c$ is the most probable time for the bubble to end, $m$ is
the exponent of the power law, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the
log-periodic oscillations. The model is linear in $A$, $B$, $C_1$ and $C_2$, so
for any given $(t_c, m, \omega)$ those four follow from least squares, and
calibration reduces to a search over three nonlinear parameters.

A calibration is admissible only if $B < 0$, which makes the growth faster than
exponential, and if the damping $D = m|B| / (\omega \sqrt{C_1^2 + C_2^2})$ is at
least $0.8$ (relaxed from the theoretical bound of 1). `fit_lppls()` enforces 
both conditions, and searches within $0.1 \le m \le 0.9$ and $6 \le \omega \le 
13$ unless told otherwise (Filimonov, Demos and Sornette 2017).

# Package overview

Every analysis starts with `fit_lppls()`, which calibrates the model to one
window of data. The other functions evaluate the model, read a calibration, move
it through time, or test it against noise.

| Task | Functions |
|:--------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| Evaluate the model | `eval_lppls()`, `SSE()` |
| Calibrate one window | `fit_lppls()` |
| Read a calibration | `print()`, `summary()`, `plot()`, `lppls_curvature()`, `residual_qq_plot()` |
| Draw a fit or a landscape | `fit_plot()`, `sse_surface_plot()`, `contour_plot_sse()` |
| Date the start of a bubble | `lppls_rolling()`, `lppls_lagrange()`, `lr_trend_test()`, `rolling_tc_plot()`, `rolling_param_plot()`, `chi_sq_np_plot()`, `chi_sq_lambda_plot()` |
| Test robustness to noise | `lppls_noise_sweep()`, `noise_param_plot()`, `noise_tc_plot()` |
| Data | `spx`, the S&P 500 daily close from 2009 to 2020 |

`fit_lppls()` has three modes. `"F1"` optimises $t_c$, $m$ and $\omega$ jointly.
`"F2"` fixes $t_c$ at each point of a grid beyond the data, optimises
$(m, \omega)$ there, and then optimises $t_c$. `"MPL"` uses the same grid to
build a modified profile likelihood for $t_c$, from which likelihood intervals
follow (Filimonov, Demos and Sornette 2017).

# Calibration of the model

First we simulate an LPPLS process with critical time at $t_c = 1001$. The simulated series ends just before the critical time.

```{r sim}
library(lpplsF)

set.seed(3630)
n_obs <- 1000
log_p <- eval_lppls(seq_len(n_obs), A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015,
                    C2 = 0.001, tc = n_obs + 1, m = 0.6, omega = 8) +
  rnorm(n_obs, sd = 0.05)
```

The landscape an optimiser has to navigate is far from simple. Below is the sum
of squared errors over $t_c$ and $\omega$ on the first 900 observations, with
every other parameter held at its true value. Along $\omega$ it oscillates
strongly, and every trough is a local minimum in which a single optimiser run
can end.

```{r landscape, dev = "png", dpi = 150, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.4, out.width = "52%"}
sse_surface_plot(log_p[1:900],
                 params = list(tc = 1001, m = 0.6, omega = 8, A = 8,
                               B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001),
                 vary = c("tc", "omega"),
                 span = list(tc = c(901, 1090), omega = c(1, 20)),
                 static = TRUE)
```

The calibration below holds out the last 100 observations, fits the first 900,
and scans the next 150 time points for $t_c$. In MPL mode every candidate $t_c$
gets its own optimisation of $(m, \omega)$, and the resulting profile becomes a
modified profile likelihood.

```{r sim-fit, comment = ""}
fit <- fit_lppls(log_p, fh = 150, hold_out = 100,
                 lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8),
                 upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                 m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1,
                 mode = "MPL", fp = TRUE, mpl_plot = TRUE)
fit
```

```{r sim-numbers, include = FALSE}
mple  <- fit$mpl_output$tc_hat_mpl
li_05 <- fit$mpl_output$LI[[1]]
```

Read the printed report before anything else, because it says whether the
numbers mean anything. Here they do. The estimate is interior, no conditional
fit sits on a bound, the conditional fits form a single cluster, and the
modified profile likelihood is defined across the whole grid, so nothing is
flagged. The MPL estimate of the critical time is `r mple`, and the widest
likelihood interval, LI(0.05), runs from `r li_05[1]` to `r li_05[2]` and
contains the true value.

```{r sim-plots}
plot(fit, "fit")
plot(fit, "mpl")
```

# Diagnostics

`spx` holds the daily close of the S&P 500 from 18 May 2009 to 31 December 2020.
The calibration below uses everything except the last 500 trading days, and
passes the calendar as `dates` so that every output shows dates as well as
in indices.

```{r spx-fit, comment = ""}
spx_fit <- fit_lppls(log(spx$close), fh = 500, hold_out = 500,
                     lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.5, 0.8),
                     upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                     m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1,
                     mode = "MPL", dates = spx$date, style = "empirical",
                     fp = TRUE)
spx_fit
```

This report ends in a list of diagnostics, and each of them limits what the
estimate can be used for. $m$ sits on its upper bound, in the point estimate and
in every conditional fit, so the estimate is a boundary solution. The regularity
conditions behind the modified profile likelihood then fail, and its intervals
are not inference. Most conditional fits ended in a clearly worse local optimum,
which one start per candidate cannot avoid; `num_searches` is the setting that
addresses it. The remaining lines explain why the intervals look so tight. They
bridge gaps in the grid, and they trace where the search happened to succeed.

```{r spx-plots}
plot(spx_fit, "fit")
plot(spx_fit, "basin")
```

None of this shows in the fit plot. The basin plot needs no extra computation,
since it is drawn from the conditional fits already stored, and it shows the
split directly: two tiers of fits instead of one smooth profile.

The flagged diagnostics do not point to a fault in the data or in the package. Boundary
solutions, split basins and an undefined likelihood are properties of the LPPLS
model itself, whose objective is non-convex and whose log-periodic parameters
are only weakly identified.

# Onset detection

The start of a bubble is as uncertain as its end. `lppls_rolling()` repeats a
calibration while the window start $T_1$ moves forward and the end $T_2$ stays
fixed. `lppls_lagrange()` then selects the start by Lagrange regularisation of
the normalised residual sum of squares (Demos and Sornette 2019), and
`lr_trend_test()` checks with a parametric bootstrap whether the trend that the
regularisation removes can be told apart from noise.

```{r rolling, eval = FALSE}
roll <- lppls_rolling(log(spx$close), t1_seq = seq(1, 501, by = 25),
                      hold_out = 500, fh = 500,
                      fit_args = list(lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.5, 0.8),
                                      upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                                      m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12,
                                      num_searches = 1, mode = "MPL"))
lag <- lppls_lagrange(roll, p = 0)
chi_sq_lambda_plot(lag)
lr_trend_test(roll, log(spx$close))
```

`lppls_noise_sweep()` asks how much noise a calibration can take before its
estimates stop meaning anything. It recalibrates a known signal at a range of
noise levels, with Gaussian innovations by default or with any generator you
supply.

```{r noise, eval = FALSE}
signal <- eval_lppls(seq_len(2000), A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015,
                     C2 = 0.001, tc = 2001, m = 0.6, omega = 8)
sweep <- lppls_noise_sweep(signal, sd_seq = seq(0.005, 0.1, by = 0.005),
                           fit_args = list(fh = 150, hold_out = 100,
                                           m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12,
                                           num_searches = 1, mode = "MPL"),
                           seed = 3630)
noise_tc_plot(sweep, true_tc = 2001)
```

Both run many calibrations, so they are shown here without output. The guided
tour on the package website runs both in full.

# Further reading

The package website, <https://mahovo.github.io/lpplsF/>, has a guided tour that
works through every function on simulated and real data, with interactive SSE
landscapes. The theory behind the calibration scheme, the modified profile
likelihood and the Lagrange regularisation is set out in the master's thesis for
which the package was written.
